headline: Appledore Ledges Give Up Cod to 8, Stripers Push the Piscataqua on the Flood
subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline doesn't sound like much until you've fished all of it — this week the shoals paid, the river paid, and the beach was the one that made you work.
body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of New Hampshire coastline and figure there's nothing to write home about. I've been running my Lund out to the Shoals for going on fifteen years and I'll tell you what — those thirteen miles fish like a hundred and thirty if you know where the bottom breaks. Appledore, the backside of Star, the humps off White Island, Broad Cove, the Piscataqua's whole tidal length up to Dover Point — that's not a short list. It's just a list nobody bothers to make because they're staring at a map instead of a fathometer.

This week the Shoals did the heavy lifting. Cod fishing off Appledore's northeast ledge has been the best of the summer so far — 60 to 85 feet of water, slack tide into the first hour of the ebb, jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of mackerel belly. Boated three keepers Tuesday morning, biggest one going 8 pounds, with a handful of shorts thrown back for good measure. Pollock are mixed in on the same drift, hitting the same jigs a little higher in the water column, which tells you the bait's stacked mid-depth right now. The mackerel are thick around Appledore and Star — jig a Sabiki rig for five minutes before you even think about groundfish and you'll have all the fresh bait you need. That's the whole trick out there. Fresh mackerel beats anything frozen you're carrying in the cooler, and the cod know the difference.

Water's held cooler here than just about anywhere south of us, and that's the reason this bite has stayed a daytime pattern instead of turning nocturnal like what's happening down in the Sound and off Jersey. Stripers south of the Cape have gone deep and gone dark, feeding mostly at night because the surface is running warm enough to shut them down during daylight. North of Cape Ann we're insulated from that — the Gulf of Maine keeps its cool, and that's kept our bass willing to feed in daylight, especially on the moving tide.

Speaking of bass — the Piscataqua has been the sleeper this week. Current there does more work than any lure you tie on, and with the tides building toward the new moon, that current's got some teeth to it now. I fished the flood off Henderson's Point and again up near Dover Point, working a white 3/4-ounce bucktail with a curl-tail trailer, bounced right along the bottom where the current seam sets up against the pilings. Picked up stripers to 28 inches doing exactly that, with a couple better fish that came unbuttoned before I could get a look at them — one of those days where the strikes felt heavier than what came to the boat. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, fished tight to structure on the last two hours of the flood, has also been putting fish in the boat for the guys anchoring up near the Memorial Bridge pilings. If you're bait fishing, don't sit and wait — reposition every twenty minutes to stay on the seam as the tide builds, because that seam moves.

Hampton Harbor's been more stop-and-go. The inlet on the incoming tide is still the play — stripers pushing bait up through the cut on the last two hours of the flood, same as every August — but it's not the volume bite it can be. I worked the channel edge off Great Boars Head with a chartreuse soft-plastic swim shad and managed two schoolies in an hour of fishing that should've produced more. The bait's there — you can see the peanut bunker balling up along the edges of the marsh — but the bass haven't committed to it the way they will once that new moon tide really starts ripping. Give it another week.

Flounder guys have had a quieter time of it, but Little Harbor and the flats inside Rye Harbor are still worth a drift with bloodworms or a piece of clam on a simple spreader rig, especially on the last of the outgoing when the water's clean. Nothing to brag about — a dinner's worth if you put in the time, not a fish story.

Bluefish are the wildcard. There's a fresh push working its way up the coast from south of the Cape, and if that continues the way it's been trending, don't be surprised if you start marking blues off Odiorne Point or even out toward the Shoals in the next week or two. I haven't seen them yet up here myself, but the signs point that direction, and when they show, they usually show fast — a slick, diving birds, and suddenly every rod on the boat is doubled over.

Looking ahead: the building tides toward the new moon should sharpen up both the Piscataqua bass bite and the Hampton Harbor push — stronger current means tighter feeding windows but better ones. At the Shoals, if the mackerel stay stacked the way they are, I'd keep running out to Appledore early, working the slack into the first hour of tide movement before the current gets too hard to hold bottom. That's been the window all week, and I don't see a reason for it to change unless the wind swings hard out of the southeast and roughs up that ledge water. Watch the forecast, but if it's clean, I'll be out there before most people's coffee's done brewing.
